message.content:
**Hydrogen – A Quick‑Reference Overview**

| Category | Property | Value / Description |
|----------|----------|---------------------|
| **Basic Atomic Data** | Atomic number | 1 |
| | Atomic mass (average) | 1.008 u |
| | Electron configuration | 1s¹ |
| | Isotopes | ¹H (protium), ²H (deuterium), ³H (tritium) |
| | Natural abundance | ¹H ≈ 99.98 %, ²H ≈ 0.02 %, ³H negligible |
| | Ionization energy | 13.598 eV (first) |
| | Electron affinity | –0.754 eV (negative → no stable anion) |
| | Electronegativity (Pauling) | 2.20 |
| | Atomic radius | 32 pm (covalent) |
| **Physical Properties (gas at 25 °C, 1 atm)** | State | Diatomic gas (H₂) |
| | Molar mass | 2.016 g mol⁻¹ |
| | Density | 0.08988 g L⁻¹ |
| | Boiling point | –252.87 °C (20.27 K) |
| | Melting point | –259.16 °C (14.00 K) |
| | Specific heat (Cp) | 28.836 J mol⁻¹ K⁻¹ |
| | Heat of vaporization | 0.431 kJ mol⁻¹ |
| | Speed of sound | ~ 1270 m s⁻¹ (at 20 °C) |
| | Compressibility factor (Z) | ~0.95 near 1 atm |
| | Solubility in water | 1.6 × 10⁻³ mol L⁻¹ (≈ 0.18 g L⁻¹) |
| **Chemical Properties** | Bond type | Covalent (H–H) |
| | Bond dissociation energy | 436 kJ mol⁻¹ |
| | Reactivity | Highly reactive; forms hydrides with metals, reacts with O₂ to form H₂O, with halogens to form HX, etc. |
| | Oxidation states | +1 (in acids, e.g., HCl), –1 (in hydrides, e.g., NaH) |
| | Acid–base behavior | Acts as a weak acid (pKa ≈ 35 for H₂O/H⁺) |
| | Combustion | 2 H₂ + O₂ → 2 H₂O (exothermic, ΔH° = –286 kJ mol⁻¹) |
| | Electrochemical potential | Standard hydrogen electrode (SHE) = 0 V |
| **Isotopic Variants** | ¹H (protium) | Stable, most abundant |
| | ²H (deuterium) | Stable, heavier isotope (mass ≈ 2.014 u) |
| | ³H (tritium) | Radioactive (β⁻ decay, t½ ≈ 12.32 y) |
| | Applications | Deuterium used in NMR, heavy water; tritium used in nuclear fusion research and luminous paints |
| **Spectroscopic Features** | Visible absorption | None (H₂ is a homonuclear diatomic with no permanent dipole) |
| | UV–Vis absorption | Lyman series (n=1→n>1) in UV |
| | Infrared absorption | Weak quadrupole transitions (e.g., 2.9 µm) |
| | Microwave transitions | 1.42 GHz (21 cm line) – key in radio astronomy |
| **Astrophysical & Energy Relevance** | Stellar fusion | Proton–proton chain (p + p → d + e⁺ + νₑ) |
| | Fusion fuel | Deuterium–tritium (D–T) reaction: D + T → He‑4 + n + 17.6 MeV |
| | Spacecraft propulsion | Liquid hydrogen + liquid oxygen (LH₂/LOX) as high‑specific‑impulse propellant |
| | Environmental impact | Clean combustion → only water vapor; no CO₂ or particulates |
| **Safety & Handling** | Flammability | Extremely flammable; flash point –45 °C |
| | Explosion limits (air) | Lower: 4 % vol, Upper: 75 % vol |
| | Toxicity | Non‑toxic; inhalation can cause hypoxia due to displacement of oxygen |
| | Storage | Requires high‑pressure cylinders (≥ 200 bar) or cryogenic tanks (–253 °C) |
| | Special precautions | Ventilation, leak detection, inert atmosphere for handling tritium |

---

### Quick Takeaways

1. **Hydrogen is the simplest element** – one proton, one electron, and (in its most common form) a diatomic molecule (H₂).
2. **It is the lightest gas** and has the lowest boiling and melting points of all elements.
3. **Its chemistry is dominated by its ability to form covalent bonds** with almost every other element, producing a vast array of compounds (water, acids, hydrides, etc.).
4. **Isotopic variants give it unique roles**: deuterium in NMR and heavy‑water reactors; tritium in nuclear fusion and radioluminescent devices.
5. **Hydrogen’s spectral lines (especially the 21 cm line)** make it a cornerstone of radio astronomy, mapping the structure of galaxies.
6. **In energy technology**, LH₂/LOX rockets and D–T fusion research highlight hydrogen’s potential as a clean, high‑energy fuel.

Feel free to ask for deeper dives into any of these aspects—whether you’re curious about hydrogen’s role in stellar nucleosynthesis, its industrial applications, or the physics behind its spectral lines!
